Peter Tragos believes that justice isn’t just a concept, it’s a process that depends on all of us. In his talk, Peter pulls back the curtain on a system most people don’t fully understand but absolutely should, because we all have a stake in how it works. Serving on a jury, Peter reminds us, is not a burden but one of the most direct and powerful ways to participate in democracy. His message is clear: do you want to be at the system’s mercy, or do you want to understand it and play a role in shaping fairness and justice? 

Peter L. Tragos is the managing partner at the Law Offices of Tragos, Sartes & Tragos in Clearwater, Florida, where he dedicates his practice to fighting for victims of wrongful death, truck and car accidents, and premises liability cases. He honed his passion for  trial work as a national champion on the Florida State University College of Law mock trial team and has since tried cases in both federal and state courts across criminal and civil matters. description:
​Millions of students need personalized college and career guidance, but overwhelmed school counselors are often responsible for hundreds of young people at once. In this talk, John Branam argues that thoughtfully designed AI coaches can help close that support gap when they work in partnership with trusted human advisors. Drawing from his own family story and the realities of inequitable access, he makes the case for humanistic AI that is affirming, secure, research-based, and built around student agency. The goal is not to replace human connection, but to give every student more of the guidance, confidence, and opportunity they deserve.

We could not do this without community support. With special thanks to the University of Oregon for their presenting partnership. Carlo Decio racconta il suo percorso personale e artistico attraverso il tema delle scelte e del rischio di non scegliere.

Partendo dalla propria esperienza da giovane incerto sul futuro, ripercorre il passaggio tra paura, aspettative sociali e ricerca della propria strada, trovando nel lavoro nel turismo e poi nel teatro una direzione inattesa ma autentica.

Il suo intervento riflette sul confronto sociale, amplificato dai social media, e sull’importanza di misurarsi solo con sé stessi. Sottolinea come i sogni non siano mete rigide ma direzioni che danno senso al cammino, e invita a non rinunciare alla propria vitalità e desiderio. 

Il messaggio centrale è un invito a scegliere con coraggio, accettare errori e cambiamenti, e vivere senza farsi guidare dalla paura o dal giudizio degli altri. Si definisce una “creativa organizzata”, perché riesce a tenere insieme molte passioni diverse che convivono nel suo percorso.

Fino a pochi anni fa era molto più introversa e indossava una sorta di “armatura” sociale. Con il tempo ha scelto di cambiare, di mettersi in gioco e di capire se questa trasformazione fosse reale anche agli occhi degli altri. Le risposte che ha ricevuto le hanno mostrato una versione di sé più eclettica, determinata e curiosa di quanto pensasse.

Oggi Stefania riconosce che non esiste una sola strada giusta: ha scelto di non seguire un percorso lineare, ma di accettare la propria complessità. In this talk, Guillermo shows us how the myths of ancient Greece are not dusty relics of the past, but a living force that continues to shape our language, our films, our video games, and our way of understanding the world. Words like panic, echo, and museum trace their roots back to the Greek gods. And stories about pride, courage, and destiny still guide our imagination centuries later. A talk that proves great myths don't die. They simply change form.

description: Why does failure leave such a lasting mark on us? Why do some setbacks break us while others become the beginning of remarkable change? Drawing on her expertise as a clinical neuropsychologist, Dr. Amina El Kefi uncovers the science behind failure and the stories we tell ourselves after it. She explains how our minds can transform disappointment into opportunity, showing that failure isn't the opposite of success—it's often the force that reshapes the narrative and opens the door to growth. Amina El Kefi is a clinical neuropsychologist, researcher, and part-time university lecturer with expertise in clinical neuropsychology. She currently serves as Monitoring & Evaluation National Coordinator at SOS Children’s Villages, combining research, teaching, and applied practice to improve child and adolescent well-being through evidence-based programs and interventions. Artificial Intelligence is transforming the world—but what powers the systems that power AI?

In this thought-provoking TEDx talk, Rajesh Mattaparthi explores a hidden frontier of artificial intelligence: the AI embedded inside the engines, generators, and industrial infrastructure that modern society depends on every day.

Drawing from his work leading AI and machine learning initiatives at Cummins, Rajesh reveals how predictive maintenance, digital twins, computer vision, and intelligent control systems are revolutionizing critical infrastructure. From school buses carrying millions of children to hospital backup generators and the power systems supporting America's rapidly expanding AI data centers, he demonstrates how machine intelligence is making the physical world safer, more resilient, and more reliable.

description:
Before trauma changes our lives, many of us have already learned what it feels like to disappear.

In this moving TEDx talk, psychologist Makeba explores the hidden connection between emotional invisibility and trauma, revealing how the absence of being truly seen can shape our relationships, resilience, and sense of self long before a traumatic event occurs. Blending powerful storytelling with psychological science, she challenges audiences to rethink healing; not as something that starts after tragedy, but as something made possible through authentic human connection.

This talk offers a profound shift in perspective: that one of the greatest gifts we can offer another person is not advice, solutions, or even words, but the experience of being genuinely seen. By understanding the psychology of connection, we can create communities where healing is no longer an individual burden but a shared human responsibility.

description: We are told that cities are the problem: crowded, dirty, destructive. Yet city life distinctly shapes behavior, and when people move to cities, consumption per capita drops dramatically. The average New Yorker consumes 74% less water, 35% less electricity, and generates 45% less garbage than the average American. When cities are designed to include nature, they become engines of biodiversity, resilience, and human well-being. In the near future, 4 in 5 people will live in cities. As we design our cities to accommodate the swell of urbanization, we have a choice. Will we squeeze nature out? Or weave nature into our places to create cities that are better, cheaper, and more resilient? Eric Sanderson is Vice President for Urban Conservation Strategy at the New York Botanical Garden.
